Posizione di dottorato nella modellazione teorica della crescita dei nanocristalli

100%, Zurigo, a tempo determinato

Contesto del progetto

Il Laboratorio di ingegneria dei materiali ottici (Prof. David J. Norris) presso il Dipartimento di ingegneria meccanica e dei processi (D-MAVT) dell'ETH Zurich studia la sintesi, la crescita, la struttura e le proprietà ottiche dei nanomateriali semiconduttori. Il nostro team interdisciplinare e internazionale combina la chimica dei materiali, la spettroscopia ottica, la microscopia elettronica, la modellazione teorica e la simulazione numerica per comprendere e controllare i materiali su scala nanometrica.

I cristalliti semiconduttori su scala nanometrica presentano proprietà ottiche (ad es., spettri di assorbimento ed emissione) che dipendono fortemente dalle loro dimensioni. Poiché questa proprietà è utile per creare materiali ottici sintonizzabili per applicazioni optoelettroniche che spaziano dai display e dalle fotocamere a infrarossi alla nanofotonica e alle tecnologie quantistiche, sono state sviluppate sintesi chimiche che producono nanocristalli a partire da vari semiconduttori. I protocolli più avanzati sono quelli che portano a particelle quasi sferiche (note come punti quantici colloidali). Tuttavia, anche i campioni di nanocristalli allo stato dell'arte presentano distribuzioni nelle dimensioni e nella morfologia delle particelle che ne limitano le prestazioni ottiche.

Due classi di nanocristalli semiconduttori costituiscono eccezioni a questa regola. Presentano una forma insolita di crescita "discreta", passando bruscamente tra una serie di dimensioni specifiche. Le nanopiastrine semiconduttrici possono essere sintetizzate con spessori uniformi a livello atomico, mentre i cosiddetti nanocristalli "di dimensioni magiche" crescono attraverso una sequenza di dimensioni ben definite. Queste osservazioni suggeriscono che potrebbero essere possibili nanocristalli con dimensioni eccezionalmente precise. Tuttavia, i meccanismi che determinano se da una specifica sintesi si formano nanopiastrine, nanocristalli di dimensioni magiche o punti quantici colloidali convenzionali rimangono poco compresi.

L'obiettivo centrale di questo progetto è sviluppare un quadro teorico universale che spieghi come emergano queste diverse modalità di crescita dei nanocristalli. La comprensione acquisita sarà utilizzata per orientare gli esperimenti verso un migliore controllo delle dimensioni, della forma e delle proprietà ottiche dei nanocristalli.

Descrizione della posizione

La persona dottoranda svilupperà descrizioni teoriche e computazionali della nucleazione e della crescita dei nanocristalli semiconduttori. Inizialmente ci si concentrerà sulla combinazione dei modelli esistenti per le nanopiastrine di CdSe e i nanocristalli di dimensioni magiche. Successivamente, il lavoro sarà ampliato per includere i punti quantici convenzionali a crescita continua e altri materiali semiconduttori, tra cui InP.

Il progetto combinerà tre approcci di modellizzazione complementari: Primo, il dottorando utilizzerà la teoria del funzionale della densità (DFT) per calcolare le energie delle superfici, dei bordi, dei gradini e dei vertici dei nanocristalli terminati da tensioattivi. Questi calcoli forniranno parametri fisicamente significativi per i modelli di crescita. Saranno inoltre utilizzati per identificare molecole tensioattive che possono stabilizzare particolari forme di nanocristalli. Secondo, il dottorando costruirà modelli di bilancio di massa che descrivono la crescita e la dissoluzione accoppiate di popolazioni di nanocristalli. Questi modelli esamineranno la crescita competitiva di nanopiastrine e nanocristalli di dimensione magica risolvendo sistemi di equazioni cinetiche accoppiate. I risultati saranno confrontati direttamente con le misure sperimentali di stabilità. I modelli saranno poi estesi per includere i punti quantici, con l'obiettivo di spiegare la transizione tra la crescita discreta e continua dei nanocristalli. Terzo, il dottorando utilizzerà simulazioni Monte Carlo cinetiche per studiare le prime fasi della crescita dei nanocristalli. Tali calcoli esamineranno come cristalliti inizialmente piccoli si sviluppino in morfologie concorrenti e come le condizioni di crescita influenzino la selezione di nanopiastrine, nanocristalli di dimensione magica o punti quantici.

Il dottorando lavorerà a stretto contatto con gli sperimentatori responsabili della sintesi dei nanocristalli e degli studi sulla crescita. Questa interazione tra teoria e sperimentazione è centrale per il progetto: i risultati sperimentali forniranno dati di input per i modelli, mentre le simulazioni guideranno la progettazione di nuovi esperimenti. I calcoli saranno eseguiti utilizzando l'infrastruttura di calcolo ad alte prestazioni di ETH Zurich. Oltre alla ricerca, il dottorando contribuirà alle attività generali di laboratorio e avrà la possibilità di partecipare alle attività didattiche e alla supervisione di studenti di bachelor e master.

Profilo

Cerchiamo un candidato curioso, motivato e autonomo, con un forte interesse per l'applicazione di metodi teorici e computazionali a problemi fondamentali della crescita dei materiali. È richiesta una solida preparazione in termodinamica, cinetica, meccanica statistica, fisica dello stato solido, chimica fisica o modellizzazione dei materiali. I candidati devono essere in possesso di, o prossimi a conseguire, una laurea magistrale in chimica, ingegneria chimica, ingegneria meccanica, scienza dei materiali, fisica, scienza computazionale o una disciplina strettamente correlata. Costituirebbe un vantaggio avere esperienza in una o più delle seguenti aree:

- Teoria del funzionale della densità e calcoli della struttura elettronica
- Monte Carlo cinetico o altri metodi di simulazione stocastica
- Soluzione numerica di equazioni differenziali o cinetiche accoppiate
- Modellazione atomistica o mesoscopica dei materiali
- Nanocristalli semiconduttori, superfici o crescita colloidale
- Programmazione scientifica
- Calcolo ad alte prestazioni

Non è richiesta un'esperienza pregressa in tutti i metodi utilizzati nel progetto. Il candidato selezionato dovrà tuttavia possedere solide basi quantitative e mostrare entusiasmo nell'apprendere nuove tecniche computazionali. Sono attesi l'eccellenza accademica, un approccio professionale alla ricerca e la capacità di lavorare in autonomia. Il candidato deve essere in grado di comunicare fluentemente in inglese, sia oralmente sia per iscritto, e dovrebbe apprezzare il lavoro in un ambiente di ricerca collaborativo e internazionale.

Offriamo

Offriamo un progetto di dottorato stimolante all'interfaccia tra teoria, calcolo e sperimentazione. Il candidato selezionato entrerà a far parte di un gruppo di ricerca collaborativo e internazionale e riceverà una formazione in diversi approcci complementari alla modellazione dei materiali. Il progetto offre opportunità di collaborazione con gruppi di ricerca esterni, accesso a strutture di calcolo avanzate, interazione con scienziati sperimentali, partecipazione a conferenze internazionali e supervisione di progetti di ricerca degli studenti.

La posizione ha sede presso il Dipartimento di ingegneria meccanica e dei processi (D-MAVT), nel campus centrale di ETH Zurich a Zurigo, in Svizzera. Lo studente avrà accesso alle risorse di calcolo ad alte prestazioni di ETH Zurich. D-MAVT è un dipartimento interdisciplinare che comprende l'ingegneria meccanica, l'ingegneria dei processi, l'ingegneria chimica e l'ingegneria biomedica, nonché la robotica e il controllo. ETH Zurich offre un ambiente scientifico eccezionale con ampie opportunità di collaborazione nei settori della scienza dei materiali, della chimica, della fisica e dell'ingegneria.

Valorizziamo la diversità e la sostenibilità

In linea con i nostri valori , ETH Zurich promuove una cultura inclusiva. Promuoviamo la parità di opportunità, valorizziamo la diversità e coltiviamo un ambiente di lavoro e di apprendimento in cui i diritti e la dignità di tutto il nostro personale e di tutti i nostri studenti siano rispettati. Visita il nostro sito web dedicato alle pari opportunità e alla diversità per scoprire come garantiamo un ambiente equo e aperto che consenta a tutti di crescere e prosperare. La sostenibilità è un valore fondamentale per noi – lavoriamo costantemente per un futuro climaticamente neutro .

Ulteriori informazioni sul nostro laboratorio sono disponibili sul nostro sito web . Le domande relative alla posizione devono essere rivolte a David J. Norris, dnorris@ethz.ch (non per le candidature).

Si noti che accettiamo esclusivamente le candidature inviate tramite il nostro portale di candidatura online. Le candidature via e-mail o per posta non saranno prese in considerazione.

Doctoral position in theoretical modeling of nanocrystal growth

100%, Zurich, fixed-term

The Optical Materials Engineering Laboratory (Prof. David J. Norris) in the Department of Mechanical and Process Engineering (D-MAVT) at ETH Zurich investigates the synthesis, growth, structure, and optical properties of semiconductor nanomaterials. Our interdisciplinary and international team combines materials chemistry, optical spectroscopy, electron microscopy, theoretical modeling, and numerical simulation to understand and control materials at the nanoscale.

Project background

Nanometer-scale semiconductor crystallites exhibit optical properties (e.g., absorption and emission spectra) that are strongly dependent on their size. Because this property is useful for creating tunable optical materials for optoelectronic applications ranging from displays and infrared cameras to nanophotonics and quantum technologies, chemical syntheses have been developed that produce nanocrystals from various semiconductors. The most advanced protocols are those that lead to quasi-spherical particles (known as colloidal quantum dots). However, even state-of-the-art nanocrystal samples contain distributions in particle size and morphology that limit their optical performance.

Two classes of semiconductor nanocrystals have been discovered as exceptions to this rule. They display an unusual form of "discrete" growth, jumping between a series of specific sizes. Semiconductor nanoplatelets can be synthesized with atomically uniform thicknesses, while so-called "magic-sized" nanocrystals grow through a sequence of well-defined sizes. These observations suggest that nanocrystals with exceptionally precise dimensions may be possible. Nevertheless, the mechanisms that govern whether nanoplatelets, magic-sized nanocrystals, or conventional colloidal quantum dots form from a specific synthesis remain poorly understood.

The central aim of this project is to develop a universal theoretical framework that explains how these different nanocrystal growth modes emerge. The resulting understanding will be used to guide experiments toward improved control over nanocrystal size, shape, and optical properties.

Job description

The doctoral student will develop theoretical and computational descriptions of the nucleation and growth of semiconductor nanocrystals. The initial focus will be on combining existing models for CdSe nanoplatelets and magic-sized nanocrystals. The work will subsequently be expanded to include conventional, continuously growing quantum dots and other semiconductor materials, including InP.

The project will combine three complementary modeling approaches: First, the student will use density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the energies of surfactant-terminated nanocrystal surfaces, edges, steps, and vertices. These calculations will provide physically meaningful parameters for the growth models. They will also be used to identify surfactant molecules that may stabilize particular nanocrystal shapes. Second, the student will construct mass-balance models describing the coupled growth and dissolution of nanocrystal populations. These models will examine the competitive growth of nanoplatelets and magic-sized nanocrystals by solving systems of coupled rate equations. The results will be compared directly with experimental stability measurements. The models will then be extended to include quantum dots, with the goal of explaining the transition between discrete and continuous nanocrystal growth. Third, the student will use kinetic Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the early stages of nanocrystal growth. Such calculations will examine how initially small crystallites develop into competing morphologies and how growth conditions influence the selection of nanoplatelets, magic-sized nanocrystals, or quantum dots.

The doctoral student will work closely with experimentalists responsible for nanocrystal synthesis and growth studies. This interaction between theory and experiment is central to the project: experimental results will provide input for the models, while simulations will guide the design of new experiments. The calculations will be performed using ETH Zurich’s high-performance computing infrastructure. In addition to research, the doctoral candidate will contribute to general laboratory activities and will have opportunities to participate in teaching and the supervision of bachelor and master’s students.

Profile

We are seeking a curious, motivated, and self-driven candidate with a strong interest in applying theoretical and computational methods to fundamental problems in materials growth. A strong background in thermodynamics, kinetics, statistical mechanics, solid-state physics, physical chemistry, or materials modeling is expected. Applicants must hold, or be close to completing, an MSc degree in chemistry, chemical engineering, mechanical engineering, materials science, physics, computational science, or a closely related discipline. Experience in one or more of the following areas would be advantageous:
• Density functional theory and electronic-structure calculations
• Kinetic Monte Carlo or other stochastic simulation methods
• Numerical solution of coupled differential or rate equations
• Atomistic or mesoscale modeling of materials
• Semiconductor nanocrystals, surfaces, or colloidal growth
• Scientific programming
• High-performance computing

Prior experience with every method used in the project is not required. The successful candidate should, however, have a strong quantitative foundation and an enthusiasm for learning new computational techniques. Academic excellence, a professional approach to research, and the ability to work independently are expected. The candidate must be able to communicate fluently in English, both orally and in writing, and should enjoy working in a collaborative and international research environment.

We offer a stimulating doctoral project at the interface of theory, computation, and experiment. The successful candidate will join a collaborative and international research group and will receive training in several complementary approaches to materials modeling. The project provides opportunities for external research collaboration, access to advanced computing facilities, interaction with experimental scientists, participation in international conferences, and the supervision of student research projects.

The position is based in the Department of Mechanical and Process Engineering (D-MAVT) at ETH Zurich’s central campus in Zurich, Switzerland. D-MAVT is an interdisciplinary department encompassing mechanical, process, chemical, and biomedical engineering, as well as robotics and control. descriptionByLocale.de:
Doktoratsstelle zur theoretischen Modellierung des Wachstums von Nanokristallen

100%, Zürich, befristet

Hintergrund des Projekts

Das Labor für optische Materialtechnik (Prof. David J. Norris) im Departement Maschinenbau und Verfahrenstechnik (D-MAVT) an der ETH Zürich untersucht die Synthese, das Wachstum, die Struktur und die optischen Eigenschaften von Halbleiter-Nanomaterialien. Unser interdisziplinäres und internationales Team verbindet Materialchemie, optische Spektroskopie, Elektronenmikroskopie, theoretische Modellierung und numerische Simulation, um Materialien auf der Nanoskala zu verstehen und zu kontrollieren.

Halbleiterkristallite im Nanometermaßstab weisen optische Eigenschaften (z. B. Absorptions- und Emissionsspektren) auf, die stark von ihrer Größe abhängen. Da diese Eigenschaft nützlich ist, um abstimmbare optische Materialien für optoelektronische Anwendungen von Displays und Infrarotkameras bis hin zu Nanophotonik und Quantentechnologien herzustellen, wurden chemische Synthesen entwickelt, mit denen Nanokristalle aus verschiedenen Halbleitern hergestellt werden. Die fortschrittlichsten Protokolle führen zu quasikugelförmigen Partikeln (bekannt als kolloidale Quantenpunkte). Allerdings weisen selbst hochmoderne Nanokristallproben Verteilungen der Partikelgröße und -morphologie auf, die ihre optische Leistungsfähigkeit begrenzen.

Als Ausnahmen von dieser Regel wurden zwei Klassen von Halbleiter-Nanokristallen entdeckt. Sie zeigen eine ungewöhnliche Form des "diskreten" Wachstums, bei der sie zwischen einer Reihe bestimmter Größen springen. Halbleiter-Nanoplättchen können mit atomar einheitlichen Dicken synthetisiert werden, während sogenannte Nanokristalle mit "magischer Größe" eine Abfolge genau definierter Größen durchlaufen. Diese Beobachtungen legen nahe, dass Nanokristalle mit außergewöhnlich präzisen Abmessungen möglich sein könnten. Dennoch sind die Mechanismen, die bestimmen, ob aus einer bestimmten Synthese Nanoplättchen, Nanokristalle mit magischer Größe oder konventionelle kolloidale Quantenpunkte entstehen, nach wie vor nur unzureichend verstanden.

Das zentrale Ziel dieses Projekts besteht darin, einen universellen theoretischen Rahmen zu entwickeln, der erklärt, wie diese unterschiedlichen Wachstumsmodi von Nanokristallen entstehen. Das daraus gewonnene Verständnis wird genutzt, um Experimente auf eine bessere Kontrolle über die Größe, Form und optischen Eigenschaften von Nanokristallen auszurichten.

Stellenbeschreibung

Die Doktorandin oder der Doktorand wird theoretische und computergestützte Beschreibungen der Keimbildung und des Wachstums von Halbleiter-Nanokristallen entwickeln. Der anfängliche Schwerpunkt wird auf der Kombination bestehender Modelle für CdSe-Nanoplättchen und Nanokristalle mit magischer Größe liegen. Anschließend wird die Arbeit auf konventionelle, kontinuierlich wachsende Quantenpunkte und andere Halbleitermaterialien, einschließlich InP, ausgeweitet.

Das Projekt wird drei einander ergänzende Modellierungsansätze kombinieren: Erstens wird die Dichtefunktionaltheorie (DFT) eingesetzt, um die Energien der mit Tensiden terminierten Oberflächen, Kanten, Stufen und Ecken von Nanokristallen zu berechnen. Diese Berechnungen werden physikalisch aussagekräftige Parameter für die Wachstumsmodelle liefern. Sie werden auch dazu verwendet, Tensidmoleküle zu identifizieren, die bestimmte Formen von Nanokristallen stabilisieren können. Zweitens werden Massenbilanzmodelle erstellt, die das gekoppelte Wachstum und die Auflösung von Nanokristallpopulationen beschreiben. Diese Modelle werden das konkurrierende Wachstum von Nanoplättchen und Nanokristallen mit magischer Größe untersuchen, indem Systeme gekoppelter Ratengleichungen gelöst werden. Die Ergebnisse werden direkt mit experimentellen Stabilitätsmessungen verglichen. Anschließend werden die Modelle um Quantenpunkte erweitert, mit dem Ziel, den Übergang zwischen diskretem und kontinuierlichem Wachstum von Nanokristallen zu erklären. Drittens werden kinetische Monte-Carlo-Simulationen eingesetzt, um die frühen Stadien des Nanokristallwachstums zu untersuchen. Mit solchen Berechnungen wird untersucht, wie sich anfänglich kleine Kristallite zu konkurrierenden Morphologien entwickeln und wie Wachstumsbedingungen die Auswahl von Nanoplättchen, Nanokristallen mit magischer Größe oder Quantenpunkten beeinflussen.

Es wird eng mit den für die Synthese von Nanokristallen und Wachstumsstudien verantwortlichen Experimentalwissenschaftlerinnen und Experimentalwissenschaftlern zusammengearbeitet. Diese Wechselwirkung zwischen Theorie und Experiment ist zentral für das Projekt: Experimentelle Ergebnisse werden den Modellen als Eingabe dienen, während Simulationen die Planung neuer Experimente leiten werden. Die Berechnungen werden unter Verwendung der Hochleistungsrecheninfrastruktur von ETH Zurich durchgeführt. Zusätzlich zur Forschung sind Beiträge zu den allgemeinen Laboraktivitäten vorgesehen; außerdem besteht die Möglichkeit, sich an der Lehre und der Betreuung von Bachelor- und Masterstudierenden zu beteiligen.

Profil

Wir suchen eine neugierige, motivierte und eigeninitiativ arbeitende Person mit großem Interesse an der Anwendung theoretischer und computergestützter Methoden auf grundlegende Probleme des Materialwachstums. Fundierte Kenntnisse in Thermodynamik, Kinetik, statistischer Mechanik, Festkörperphysik, physikalischer Chemie oder Materialmodellierung werden erwartet. Bewerbende müssen über einen MSc-Abschluss in Chemie, Chemieingenieurwesen, Maschinenbau, Materialwissenschaften, Physik, Computational Science oder einer eng verwandten Fachrichtung verfügen oder kurz vor dessen Abschluss stehen. Erfahrungen in einem oder mehreren der folgenden Bereiche wären von Vorteil:

- Dichtefunktionaltheorie und Berechnungen zur elektronischen Struktur
- Kinetisches Monte-Carlo-Verfahren oder andere stochastische Simulationsmethoden
- Numerische Lösung gekoppelter Differential- oder Ratengleichungen
- Atomistische oder mesoskalige Modellierung von Materialien
- Halbleiter-Nanokristalle, Oberflächen oder kolloidales Wachstum
- Wissenschaftliches Programmieren
- Hochleistungsrechnen

Vorherige Erfahrung mit jeder der im Projekt verwendeten Methoden ist nicht erforderlich. Die ausgewählte Person sollte jedoch über eine solide quantitative Grundlage verfügen und Begeisterung dafür mitbringen, neue computergestützte Techniken zu erlernen. Akademische Exzellenz, eine professionelle Herangehensweise an die Forschung und die Fähigkeit zum selbstständigen Arbeiten werden erwartet. Es wird vorausgesetzt, dass die Person sowohl mündlich als auch schriftlich fließend auf Englisch kommunizieren kann und gerne in einem kooperativen und internationalen Forschungsumfeld arbeitet.

Wir bieten

Wir bieten Ihnen ein spannendes Promotionsprojekt an der Schnittstelle von Theorie, Berechnung und Experiment. Bei erfolgreicher Bewerbung treten Sie einer kooperativen und internationalen Forschungsgruppe bei und werden in mehreren sich ergänzenden Ansätzen der Materialmodellierung ausgebildet. Das Projekt bietet Ihnen Möglichkeiten zur Zusammenarbeit mit externen Forschungspartnern, Zugang zu hochmodernen Recheninfrastrukturen, Austausch mit experimentell arbeitenden Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftlern, Teilnahme an internationalen Konferenzen und die Betreuung von Forschungsprojekten Studierender.

Die Stelle ist im Departement Maschinenbau und Verfahrenstechnik (D-MAVT) auf dem zentralen Campus der ETH Zurich in Zürich, Schweiz, angesiedelt. Sie erhalten Zugang zu den Ressourcen der ETH Zurich für Hochleistungsrechnen. Das D-MAVT ist ein interdisziplinäres Departement, das Maschinenbau, Verfahrenstechnik, Chemieingenieurwesen und Biomedizintechnik sowie Robotik und Regelungstechnik umfasst. Die ETH Zurich bietet ein herausragendes wissenschaftliches Umfeld mit umfangreichen Möglichkeiten zur Zusammenarbeit in den Bereichen Materialwissenschaften, Chemie, Physik und Ingenieurwissenschaften.

Wir schätzen Vielfalt und Nachhaltigkeit

Im Einklang mit unseren Werten , fördert die ETH Zurich eine inklusive Kultur. descriptionByLocale.fr:
Poste doctoral en modélisation théorique de la croissance des nanocristaux

100%, Zurich, à durée déterminée

Contexte du projet

Le Laboratoire d'ingénierie des matériaux optiques (Prof. David J. Norris) du Département de génie mécanique et des procédés (D-MAVT) de l'ETH Zurich étudie la synthèse, la croissance, la structure et les propriétés optiques des nanomatériaux semi-conducteurs. Notre équipe interdisciplinaire et internationale associe la chimie des matériaux, la spectroscopie optique, la microscopie électronique, la modélisation théorique et la simulation numérique afin de comprendre et de contrôler les matériaux à l'échelle nanométrique.

Les cristallites semi-conducteurs de taille nanométrique présentent des propriétés optiques (par exemple, des spectres d'absorption et d'émission) qui dépendent fortement de leur taille. Cette propriété étant utile pour créer des matériaux optiques accordables destinés à des applications optoélectroniques allant des écrans et des caméras infrarouges à la nanophotonique et aux technologies quantiques, des synthèses chimiques ont été mises au point pour produire des nanocristaux à partir de divers semi-conducteurs. Les protocoles les plus avancés sont ceux qui conduisent à des particules quasi sphériques (appelées points quantiques colloïdaux). Cependant, même les échantillons de nanocristaux les plus avancés présentent des distributions de taille et de morphologie des particules qui limitent leurs performances optiques.

Deux classes de nanocristaux semi-conducteurs ont été découvertes qui font exception à cette règle. Elles présentent une forme inhabituelle de croissance « discrète », avec des sauts entre une série de tailles spécifiques. Les nanoplaquettes semi-conductrices peuvent être synthétisées avec des épaisseurs uniformes à l'échelle atomique, tandis que les nanocristaux dits « de taille magique » croissent selon une séquence de tailles bien définies. Ces observations suggèrent qu'il pourrait être possible d'obtenir des nanocristaux aux dimensions exceptionnellement précises. Néanmoins, les mécanismes qui régissent la formation, à partir d'une synthèse donnée, de nanoplaquettes, de nanocristaux de taille magique ou de points quantiques colloïdaux conventionnels restent mal compris.

L'objectif central de ce projet est de développer un cadre théorique universel qui explique comment apparaissent ces différents modes de croissance des nanocristaux. La compréhension qui en résultera servira à orienter les expériences vers un meilleur contrôle de la taille, de la forme et des propriétés optiques des nanocristaux.

Description du poste

La personne doctorante développera des descriptions théoriques et numériques de la nucléation et de la croissance des nanocristaux semi-conducteurs. L'accent initial sera mis sur la combinaison de modèles existants pour les nanoplaquettes de CdSe et les nanocristaux de taille magique. Le travail sera ensuite étendu pour inclure des points quantiques conventionnels à croissance continue et d'autres matériaux semi-conducteurs, notamment l'InP.

Le projet combinera trois approches de modélisation complémentaires : Premièrement, l’étudiant utilisera la théorie de la fonctionnelle de la densité (DFT) pour calculer les énergies des surfaces, arêtes, marches et sommets de nanocristaux terminés par des tensioactifs. Ces calculs fourniront des paramètres physiquement pertinents pour les modèles de croissance. Ils serviront également à identifier des molécules tensioactives susceptibles de stabiliser certaines formes de nanocristaux. Deuxièmement, l’étudiant construira des modèles de bilan de matière décrivant la croissance et la dissolution couplées de populations de nanocristaux. Ces modèles examineront la croissance compétitive des nanoplaquettes et des nanocristaux de taille magique en résolvant des systèmes d’équations cinétiques couplées. Les résultats seront comparés directement aux mesures expérimentales de stabilité. Les modèles seront ensuite étendus pour inclure les boîtes quantiques, dans le but d’expliquer la transition entre la croissance discrète et continue des nanocristaux. Troisièmement, l’étudiant utilisera des simulations de Monte Carlo cinétique pour étudier les premiers stades de la croissance des nanocristaux. De tels calculs examineront comment des cristallites initialement petits évoluent vers des morphologies concurrentes et comment les conditions de croissance influencent la sélection de nanoplaquettes, de nanocristaux de taille magique ou de boîtes quantiques.

L’étudiant en doctorat travaillera en étroite collaboration avec les expérimentateurs responsables de la synthèse des nanocristaux et des études de croissance. Cette interaction entre la théorie et l’expérience est au cœur du projet : les résultats expérimentaux fourniront des données d’entrée aux modèles, tandis que les simulations guideront la conception de nouvelles expériences. Les calculs seront effectués à l’aide de l’infrastructure de calcul haute performance de l’ETH Zurich. En plus de ses activités de recherche, la personne doctorante contribuera aux activités générales du laboratoire et aura l’occasion de participer à l’enseignement et à l’encadrement d’étudiants de bachelor et de master.

Profil

Nous recherchons une personne curieuse, motivée et autonome, vivement intéressée par l’application de méthodes théoriques et computationnelles à des problèmes fondamentaux de croissance des matériaux. Une solide formation en thermodynamique, cinétique, mécanique statistique, physique du solide, chimie physique ou modélisation des matériaux est attendue. Les personnes candidates doivent être titulaires d’un diplôme de MSc en chimie, génie chimique, génie mécanique, science des matériaux, physique, science computationnelle ou dans une discipline étroitement apparentée, ou être sur le point de l’obtenir. Une expérience dans un ou plusieurs des domaines suivants constituerait un atout :

- Théorie de la fonctionnelle de la densité et calculs de structure électronique
- Méthode de Monte Carlo cinétique ou autres méthodes de simulation stochastique
- Résolution numérique d'équations différentielles couplées ou d'équations de taux
- Modélisation atomistique ou mésoscopique des matériaux
- Nanocristaux semi-conducteurs, surfaces ou croissance colloïdale
- Programmation scientifique
- Calcul haute performance

Il n'est pas nécessaire d'avoir une expérience préalable de chacune des méthodes utilisées dans le projet. La personne retenue devra toutefois disposer de solides bases quantitatives et être enthousiaste à l'idée d'apprendre de nouvelles techniques computationnelles. L'excellence académique, une approche professionnelle de la recherche et la capacité à travailler de manière autonome sont attendues. La personne candidate doit être capable de communiquer couramment en anglais, tant à l'oral qu'à l'écrit, et devrait aimer travailler dans un environnement de recherche collaboratif et international.

Nous offrons

Nous proposons un projet doctoral stimulant à l'interface de la théorie, du calcul et de l'expérimentation. La personne retenue rejoindra un groupe de recherche collaboratif et international et bénéficiera d'une formation à plusieurs approches complémentaires de la modélisation des matériaux. Le projet offre des possibilités de collaboration avec des équipes de recherche externes, un accès à des infrastructures de calcul avancées, des échanges avec des scientifiques expérimentaux, la participation à des conférences internationales et l'encadrement de projets de recherche d'étudiants.

Le poste est basé au Département de génie mécanique et des procédés (D-MAVT), sur le campus central d'ETH Zurich à Zurich, en Suisse. La personne doctorante aura accès aux ressources de calcul haute performance d'ETH Zurich. Le D-MAVT est un département interdisciplinaire englobant le génie mécanique, le génie des procédés, le génie chimique et le génie biomédical, ainsi que la robotique et l'automatique. ETH Zurich offre un environnement scientifique exceptionnel, avec de nombreuses possibilités de collaboration dans les domaines de la science des matériaux, de la chimie, de la physique et de l'ingénierie.

Nous attachons de l’importance à la diversité et à la durabilité

Conformément à nos valeurs , ETH Zurich encourage une culture inclusive. Nous favorisons l'égalité des chances, valorisons la diversité et cultivons un environnement de travail et d'apprentissage dans lequel les droits et la dignité de l'ensemble de notre personnel et de nos étudiants sont respectés. Consultez notre site web consacré à l'égalité des chances et à la diversité pour découvrir comment nous garantissons un environnement équitable et ouvert qui permet à chacun de s'épanouir et de prospérer. La durabilité est une valeur fondamentale pour nous – nous œuvrons constamment en faveur d'un avenir climatiquement neutre .

Vous êtes curieux ? Nous aussi.

Nous nous réjouissons de recevoir votre candidature en ligne avec les documents suivants, réunis en un seul PDF :

- Une lettre de motivation décrivant votre motivation pour le poste, votre expérience de recherche pertinente et vos principales réalisations scientifiques à ce jour (deux pages maximum)
- Un CV
- Diplômes et relevés de notes
- Coordonnées d’au moins trois références universitaires ou professionnelles

De plus amples informations sur notre laboratoire sont disponibles sur notre site web . Les questions relatives au poste doivent être adressées à David J. Norris, dnorris@ethz.ch (pas de candidatures).

Veuillez noter que nous acceptons exclusivement les candidatures soumises par l'intermédiaire de notre portail de candidature en ligne. Les candidatures envoyées par e-mail ou par voie postale ne seront pas prises en considération.

Nous recrutons une personne doctorante à temps plein pour développer des modèles théoriques et computationnels de la croissance de nanocristaux semi-conducteurs, avec une date de début prévue à partir du 1er octobre 2026.

Le poste doctoral est prévu pour quatre ans à un taux d'occupation de 100% et sera supervisé par le Prof. Dr. David J. Norris. Le poste est subordonné à l'admission au programme doctoral d'ETH Zurich.

À propos de l’ETH Zürich

ETH Zurich est l'une des principales universités au monde spécialisées dans
la science et la technologie. Nous sommes réputés pour notre enseignement d'excellence,
notre recherche fondamentale de pointe et le transfert direct de nouvelles connaissances
dans la société. Plus de 30,000 personnes originaires de plus de 120 pays considèrent notre
université comme un lieu qui favorise la pensée indépendante et un
environnement qui inspire l’excellence. Située au cœur de l’Europe,
tout en tissant des liens partout dans le monde, nous travaillons ensemble pour
élaborer des solutions aux défis mondiaux d’aujourd’hui et de demain.

jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in mechanics of frictional particle suspensions

100%, Zurich, fixed-term

At the Professorship of Solid Mechanics (SMEC) in the Institute for Building Materials at ETH Zurich, we aim to understand how materials deform, degrade, break, and ultimately fail. Our research is driven by curiosity about the physical mechanisms that underlie failure and by the ambition to translate this understanding into more reliable and resilient materials and structures. By combining numerical modeling, laboratory experiments, and theoretical analyses, we seek to link microscopic processes with the macroscopic behavior of both engineering and natural systems and develop predictive tools for mechanical failure.

Our team is highly interdisciplinary and international, bringing together researchers with backgrounds in materials science, mechanics, and applied physics. We work across a broad range of topics, including the mechanics of particle systems (colloidal and granular), architected and topologically interlocked materials, the mechanics of fragility in collagen, the mechanics of earthquakes, fracture of soft materials, and modeling failure in multiphysical processes such as corrosion-driven degradation of concrete. What unites these efforts is a shared curiosity about why complex materials fail and a commitment to developing new concepts, experiments, and models that advance our understanding of failure mechanics.

We are seeking a motivated, innovative doctoral student with a strong interest in mechanics and applied physics to investigate how microscopic frictional interactions govern the macroscopic behavior of dense particle suspensions. The central challenge is to understand how sliding and rolling friction, individually and in combination, shape the rheological response across scales. The project combines physics-based modeling, simulation, theoretical reasoning, and quantitative comparison with experiments in collaboration with partners from the ETH Department of Materials.

Job description
• You will conduct a computational and theoretical investigation of how particle-scale frictional interactions govern the macroscopic flow response of concentrated suspensions.
• The work will connect particle-scale mechanics, including particle geometry and frictional interactions, with the collective and macroscopic response of the suspension using physics-based models.
• You will implement and use particle-based simulation methods, including coarse-grained molecular dynamics, and perform rigorous verification and validation using datasets provided by our collaborators.
• You will analyze simulation results to identify the physical mechanisms controlling the suspension response and work in close collaboration with experimental researchers within the project, providing modeling insights and helping to interpret experimental observations.
• The position provides a stimulating environment for scientific growth and collaboration.

Profile
• You hold an MSc degree in mechanics, physics, (civil, mechanical, aerospace, or bio-) engineering, material science, or a related discipline.
• You have a background in mechanics, applied physics, computational mechanics, scientific computing, or a related field. A foundation in areas such as solid mechanics, fluid mechanics, dynamics, or numerical modeling is particularly relevant.
• You have experience implementing scientific code and assessing computational results through validation, verification, and quantitative comparison with reference data.
• You have prior programming experience in Python and have used version control.
• You are curious, self-motivated, and interested in using modeling and quantitative reasoning to answer mechanics and physics questions. You enjoy connecting computational work with experiments and collaborating closely with experimentalists. Experience with colloidal suspensions, rheology, or coarse-grained molecular dynamics is an advantage but is not required; the project-specific methods and concepts can be learned during the doctoral studies.
• You are fluent in English (oral and written).
• You enjoy working in a team, possess the necessary social skills and communication abilities, and contribute proactively to a positive group atmosphere.

We offer
• You will join a dynamic, international, and supportive research group that values curiosity, rigor, and collaboration.
• Your job with impact: Become part of ETH Zurich, which not only supports your professional development, but also actively contributes to positive change in society.
• We are actively committed to a sustainable and climate-neutral university .
• You can expect numerous benefits , such as public transport season tickets and car sharing, a wide range of sports offered by the ASVZ , childcare and attractive pension benefits .

We value diversity and sustainability

In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. We promote equality of opportunity, value diversity and nurture a working and learning environment in which the rights and dignity of all our staff and students are respected. Visit our Equal Opportunities and Diversity website to find out how we ensure a fair and open environment that allows everyone to grow and flourish. Sustainability is a core value for us – we are consistently working towards a climate-neutral future .

Curious? So are we.

We look forward to receiving your online application with the following documents:
• CV
• An academic transcript/list of courses completed
• A brief statement describing your project idea relevant to the job description, making a connection to your experience and the related work from the literature
• The names and contact details of two references

Further information about the professorship can be found on our website . Questions regarding the position should be directed to Prof. David Kammer, dkammer@ethz.ch (no applications).

Please note that we exclusively accept applications submitted through our online application portal. Applications via email or postal services will not be considered.

We would like to point out that the pre-selection is carried out by the responsible recruiters and not by artificial intelligence.

The position is available with a flexible start date, possibly as soon as possible.

About ETH Zürich

ETH Zurich is one of the world’s leading universities specialising in
science and technology. We are renowned for our excellent education,
cutting-edge fundamental research and direct transfer of new knowledge
into society. Over 30,000 people from more than 120 countries find our
university to be a place that promotes independent thinking and an
environment that inspires excellence. Located in the heart of Europe,
yet forging connections all over the world, we work together to
develop solutions for the global challenges of today and tomorrow.

Posizione Dottorale in meccanica delle sospensioni di particelle attrito

100%, Zurigo, a tempo determinato

Alla cattedra di Solid Mechanics (SMEC) dell'Istituto per i materiali da costruzione dell'ETH di Zurigo, ci proponiamo di capire come i materiali deformano, degradano, si rompono e infine falliscono. La nostra ricerca è guidata dalla curiosità sui meccanismi fisici che sottomettono al fallimento e dall'ambizione di tradurre questa comprensione in materiali e strutture più affidabili e resilienti. Combinando la modellazione numerica, gli esperimenti di laboratorio e le analisi teoriche, cerchiamo di collegare i processi microscopici con il comportamento macroscopico dei sistemi ingegneristici e naturali e di sviluppare strumenti predittivi per il fallimento meccanico.

Il nostro team è altamente interdisciplinare e internazionale, che riunisce ricercatori con sfondi in scienza dei materiali, meccanica e fisica applicata. Lavoriamo attraverso una vasta gamma di argomenti, tra cui la meccanica dei sistemi di particelle (colloidale e granulare), materiali progettati e topologicamente interlocked, la meccanica della fragilità nel collagene, la meccanica dei terremoti, la frattura dei materiali morbidi e la modellazione del fallimento nei processi multifisici come la degradazione del cemento a corrosione. Ciò che unisce questi sforzi è una curiosità condivisa sul perché i materiali complessi falliscono e l'impegno a sviluppare nuovi concetti, esperimenti e modelli che avanzano la nostra comprensione della meccanica fallita.

Stiamo cercando uno studente medico motivato e innovativo con un forte interesse per la meccanica e la fisica applicata per indagare come le interazioni microscopiche attrito governano il comportamento macroscopico delle sospensioni dense di particelle. La sfida centrale è capire come l'attrito scorrevole e rotolante, individualmente e in combinazione, modellare la risposta reologica su scala. Il progetto combina la modellazione fisica, la simulazione, il ragionamento teorico e il confronto quantitativo con esperimenti in collaborazione con partner del Dipartimento dei Materiali ETH.

Descrizione del lavoro
• Condurrai un'indagine computazionale e teorica su come le interazioni attrito su scala delle particelle governano la risposta del flusso macroscopico delle sospensioni concentrate.
• Il lavoro collegherà la meccanica delle particelle, compresa la geometria delle particelle e le interazioni attrito, con la risposta collettiva e macroscopica della sospensione utilizzando modelli basati sulla fisica.
• Realizzerai e userai metodi di simulazione basati sulle particelle, tra cui dinamiche molecolari grossolane, e eseguirai una rigorosa verifica e validazione utilizzando i dataset forniti dai nostri collaboratori.
• Analizzerai i risultati della simulazione per identificare i meccanismi fisici che controllano la risposta delle sospensioni e lavoreranno in stretta collaborazione con ricercatori sperimentali all'interno del progetto, fornendo spunti di modellazione e aiutando a interpretare osservazioni sperimentali.
• La posizione offre un ambiente stimolante per la crescita scientifica e la collaborazione.

Profilo
• Hai una laurea in meccanica, fisica, (civile, meccanico, aerospaziale, o bio-) ingegneria, scienza materiale, o una disciplina correlata.
• Hai un background in meccanica, fisica applicata, meccanica computazionale, informatica scientifica, o un campo correlato. Una fondazione in aree come meccanica solida, meccanica fluida, dinamica o modellazione numerica è particolarmente rilevante.
• Hai esperienza nell'attuazione del codice scientifico e nella valutazione dei risultati computazionali attraverso la convalida, la verifica e il confronto quantitativo con i dati di riferimento.
• Hai esperienza di programmazione precedente in Python e hai usato il controllo della versione.
• Siete curiosi, auto-motivati, e interessati ad utilizzare la modellazione e il ragionamento quantitativo per rispondere a domande di meccanica e fisica. Ti piace collegare il lavoro computazionale con gli esperimenti e collaborare strettamente con gli sperimentatori. L'esperienza con sospensioni colloidali, reologia o dinamiche molecolari grossolane è un vantaggio ma non è richiesto; i metodi e i concetti specifici del progetto possono essere appresi durante gli studi di dottorato.
• Sei fluente in inglese (orale e scritto).
• Ti piace lavorare in un team, possedere le competenze sociali e le capacità di comunicazione necessarie, e contribuire in modo proattivo ad un'atmosfera di gruppo positiva.

Offriamo
• Ti unirai a un gruppo di ricerca dinamico, internazionale e di supporto che valorizza curiosità, rigore e collaborazione.
• Il tuo lavoro con impatto: Diventa parte dell'ETH di Zurigo, che non solo supporta lo sviluppo professionale, ma contribuisce attivamente al cambiamento positivo nella società.
• Siamo attivamente impegnati in un'università sostenibile e neutrale dal clima.
• Puoi aspettarti numerosi vantaggi, come i biglietti per la stagione dei trasporti pubblici e la condivisione delle auto, una vasta gamma di sport offerti dalla ASVZ , l'assistenza all'infanzia e le interessanti prestazioni pensionistiche.

Apprezziamo la diversità e la sostenibilità

In linea con i nostri valori, ETH Zurich incoraggia una cultura inclusiva. Promuoviamo l'uguaglianza di opportunità, la diversità di valore e nutrire un ambiente di lavoro e di apprendimento in cui i diritti e la dignità di tutto il nostro staff e gli studenti sono rispettati. Visita il nostro sito web Equal Opportunities and Diversity per scoprire come garantiamo un ambiente equo e aperto che permetta a tutti di crescere e fiorire. La sostenibilità è un valore fondamentale per noi – stiamo costantemente lavorando verso un futuro neutro dal clima.

Curioso? Anche noi.

Non vediamo l'ora di ricevere la tua domanda online con i seguenti documenti:
• CV
• Una trascrizione accademica/lista dei corsi completati
• Una breve dichiarazione che descrive la vostra idea di progetto relativa alla descrizione del lavoro, rendendo un legame con la vostra esperienza e il relativo lavoro dalla letteratura
• I nomi e i dettagli di contatto di due riferimenti

Ulteriori informazioni sulla cattedra possono essere trovate sul nostro sito web . Le domande relative alla posizione devono essere indirizzate al Prof. David Kammer, dkammer@ethz.ch (nessuna domanda).

Si prega di notare che accettiamo esclusivamente le applicazioni inviate tramite il nostro portale di applicazioni online. Le applicazioni via e-mail o servizi postali non saranno considerate.

Vorremmo sottolineare che la pre-selezione è effettuata dai reclutatori responsabili e non dall'intelligenza artificiale.

La posizione è disponibile con una data di inizio flessibile, possibilmente il prima possibile.

Informazioni su ETH Zürich

ETH Zurich è una delle università più importanti del mondo specializzata in
scienza e tecnologia. Siamo rinomati per la nostra eccellente educazione,
ricerca fondamentale all'avanguardia e trasferimento diretto di nuove conoscenze
nella società. Oltre 30.000 persone provenienti da più di 120 paesi
università per essere un luogo che promuove il pensiero indipendente e un
ambiente che ispira eccellenza. Situato nel cuore dell'Europa,
ancora forgiando connessioni in tutto il mondo, lavoriamo insieme a
sviluppare soluzioni per le sfide globali di oggi e domani.

Promotionsposition in der Mechanik von Reibungspartikelsuspensionen

100%, Zürich, befristet

An der Professur für Festkörpermechanik (SMEC) am Institut für Baustoffe der ETH Zürich wollen wir verstehen, wie sich Materialien verformen, abbauen, brechen und letztlich versagen. Unsere Forschung basiert auf der Neugier auf die physikalischen Mechanismen, die dem Versagen zugrunde liegen, und auf dem Ehrgeiz, dieses Verständnis in zuverlässigere und belastbarere Materialien und Strukturen umzusetzen. Durch die Kombination von numerischer Modellierung, Laborexperimenten und theoretischen Analysen versuchen wir, mikroskopische Prozesse mit dem makroskopischen Verhalten sowohl von technischen als auch von natürlichen Systemen zu verbinden und prädiktive Werkzeuge für mechanisches Versagen zu entwickeln.

Unser Team ist in hohem Maße interdisziplinär und international und bringt Forscher mit Hintergründen aus den Bereichen Materialwissenschaft, Mechanik und angewandte Physik zusammen. Wir arbeiten über ein breites Spektrum von Themen, einschließlich der Mechanik von Partikelsystemen (kolloidal und granular), architektonischen und topologisch ineinandergreifenden Materialien, der Mechanik der Fragilität in Kollagen, der Mechanik von Erdbeben, des Bruchs weicher Materialien und des Modellierungsversagens in multiphysikalischen Prozessen wie dem korrosionsbedingten Abbau von Beton. Was diese Bemühungen verbindet, ist die gemeinsame Neugierde, warum komplexe Materialien versagen, und die Verpflichtung, neue Konzepte, Experimente und Modelle zu entwickeln, die unser Verständnis der Fehlermechanik verbessern.

Wir suchen einen motivierten, innovativen Doktoranden mit einem starken Interesse an Mechanik und angewandter Physik, um zu untersuchen, wie mikroskopische Reibungswechselwirkungen das makroskopische Verhalten dichter Partikelsuspensionen steuern. Die zentrale Herausforderung besteht darin, zu verstehen, wie Gleitreibung und Rollreibung einzeln und in Kombination die rheologische Reaktion über Skalen hinweg beeinflussen. Das Projekt kombiniert physikbasierte Modellierung, Simulation, theoretisches Denken und quantitativen Vergleich mit Experimenten in Zusammenarbeit mit Partnern der ETH-Abteilung Werkstoffe.

Stellenbeschreibung
• Sie werden eine rechnerische und theoretische Untersuchung durchführen, wie Reibungswechselwirkungen im Teilchenmaßstab die makroskopische Strömungsreaktion konzentrierter Suspensionen steuern.
• Die Arbeit wird die Mechanik im Teilchenmaßstab, einschließlich der Teilchengeometrie und Reibungswechselwirkungen, mit der kollektiven und makroskopischen Reaktion der Suspension unter Verwendung physikbasierter Modelle verbinden.
• Sie implementieren und verwenden partikelbasierte Simulationsmethoden, einschließlich grobkörniger Molekulardynamik, und führen eine strenge Verifizierung und Validierung unter Verwendung von Datensätzen durch, die von unseren Mitarbeitern bereitgestellt werden.
• Sie werden Simulationsergebnisse analysieren, um die physikalischen Mechanismen zu identifizieren, die die Suspensionsreaktion steuern, und in enger Zusammenarbeit mit experimentellen Forschern innerhalb des Projekts arbeiten, Modellierungserkenntnisse liefern und bei der Interpretation experimenteller Beobachtungen helfen.
• Die Position bietet ein stimulierendes Umfeld für wissenschaftliche Wachstum und Zusammenarbeit.

Profil
• Sie haben einen MSc-Abschluss in Mechanik, Physik, (Zivil-, Mechanik-, Luft- und Raumfahrt- oder Bio-) Ingenieurwesen, Materialwissenschaften oder einer verwandten Disziplin.
• Sie haben einen Hintergrund in Mechanik, angewandter Physik, Computermechanik, wissenschaftlichem Computing oder einem verwandten Bereich. Eine Grundlage in Bereichen wie Festkörpermechanik, Strömungsmechanik, Dynamik oder numerische Modellierung ist besonders relevant.
• Sie haben Erfahrung in der Implementierung von wissenschaftlichen Codes und der Bewertung von Rechenergebnissen durch Validierung, Verifizierung und quantitativen Vergleich mit Referenzdaten.

Erfahrungen mit kolloidalen Suspensionen, Rheologie oder grobkörniger Molekulardynamik sind von Vorteil, aber nicht erforderlich; die projektspezifischen Methoden und Konzepte können während des Promotionsstudiums erlernt werden.

descriptionByLocale.fr:
Position au doctorat dans la mécanique des suspensions de particules à friction

100%, Zurich, durée déterminée

Au Professeur de Mécanique Solide (SMEC) à l'Institut des matériaux de construction à l'ETH Zurich, nous voulons comprendre comment les matériaux déforment, dégradent, brisent et finalement échouent. Nos recherches sont motivées par la curiosité au sujet des mécanismes physiques qui sous-tendent l'échec et par l'ambition de traduire cette compréhension en matériaux et structures plus fiables et plus résistants. En combinant la modélisation numérique, les expériences de laboratoire et les analyses théoriques, nous cherchons à lier les processus microscopiques au comportement macroscopique des systèmes d'ingénierie et des systèmes naturels et à développer des outils prédictifs pour la défaillance mécanique.

Notre équipe est hautement interdisciplinaire et internationale, réunissant des chercheurs ayant des connaissances en sciences des matériaux, en mécanique et en physique appliquée. Nous travaillons sur un large éventail de sujets, y compris la mécanique des systèmes de particules (colloïdaux et granulaires), les matériaux architecturés et topologiques entrelacés, la mécanique de la fragilité du collagène, la mécanique des tremblements de terre, la fracture des matériaux mous et l'échec de la modélisation dans des processus multiphysiques tels que la dégradation du béton par la corrosion. Ce qui unit ces efforts est une curiosité commune sur la raison pour laquelle les matériaux complexes échouent et un engagement à développer de nouveaux concepts, expériences et modèles qui font progresser notre compréhension de la mécanique de défaillance.

Nous recherchons un doctorant motivé et innovant qui s'intéresse fortement à la mécanique et à la physique appliquée pour étudier comment les interactions de friction microscopique régissent le comportement macroscopique des suspensions de particules denses. Le défi central est de comprendre comment la friction coulissante et la friction de roulement, individuellement et en combinaison, façonnent la réponse rhéologique à travers les échelles. Le projet combine modélisation physique, simulation, raisonnement théorique et comparaison quantitative avec des expériences en collaboration avec des partenaires du Département des matériaux de l'ETH.

Description du poste
• Vous effectuerez une étude calculatrice et théorique de la façon dont les interactions de friction à l'échelle des particules régissent la réponse du flux macroscopique des suspensions concentrées.
• Le travail reliera la mécanique à l'échelle des particules, y compris la géométrie des particules et les interactions de friction, à la réponse collective et macroscopique de la suspension à l'aide de modèles basés sur la physique.
• Vous appliquerez et utiliserez des méthodes de simulation basées sur les particules, y compris la dynamique moléculaire à grains grossiers, et effectuerez une vérification et une validation rigoureuses à l'aide des ensembles de données fournis par nos collaborateurs.
• Vous analyserez les résultats de simulation afin d'identifier les mécanismes physiques qui contrôlent la réponse à la suspension et travaillerez en étroite collaboration avec des chercheurs expérimentaux dans le cadre du projet, fournissant des idées de modélisation et aidant à interpréter les observations expérimentales.
• La position offre un environnement stimulant pour la croissance et la collaboration scientifiques.

Profil
• Vous êtes titulaire d'une maîtrise en mécanique, en physique, en génie (civil, mécanique, aérospatial ou bio-), en sciences matérielles ou dans une discipline connexe.
• Vous avez une formation en mécanique, physique appliquée, mécanique informatique, informatique scientifique ou un domaine connexe. Une fondation dans des domaines comme la mécanique solide, la mécanique des fluides, la dynamique ou la modélisation numérique est particulièrement pertinente.
• Vous avez de l'expérience dans la mise en oeuvre du code scientifique et l'évaluation des résultats de calcul par la validation, la vérification et la comparaison quantitative avec les données de référence.
• Vous avez déjà une expérience de programmation en Python et avez utilisé le contrôle de version.
• Vous êtes curieux, motivé et intéressé à utiliser la modélisation et le raisonnement quantitatif pour répondre à des questions de mécanique et de physique. Vous aimez connecter le travail computationnel avec les expériences et collaborer étroitement avec les expérimentationnistes. L'expérience des suspensions colloïdales, de la rhéologie ou de la dynamique moléculaire à grains grossiers est un avantage, mais elle n'est pas requise; les méthodes et les concepts propres au projet peuvent être apprises pendant les études doctorales.
• Vous parlez couramment anglais (oral et écrit).
• Vous aimez travailler en équipe, posséder les compétences sociales et les capacités de communication nécessaires, et contribuer de façon proactive à une atmosphère de groupe positive.

Nous offrons
• Vous rejoindrez un groupe de recherche dynamique, international et solidaire qui valorise la curiosité, la rigueur et la collaboration.
• Votre travail avec impact: Devenez membre de l'ETH Zurich, qui non seulement soutient votre développement professionnel, mais contribue également activement au changement positif dans la société.

The position is expected to start in January 2027 and is fully funded for 4 years.

This is an SNSF funded project that aims to improve our understanding and management of debris flows, which are one of the most important hazards in mountainous areas. The project is focussed on collecting and analyzing a unique field data se t collected using sensors originally developed for mobile robotics applications.

Job description
• Particular focus will be placed on deriving velocity and flow depth estimates at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions by analyzing point cloud and camera data
• You will develop a deep understanding of debris flow motion, and use this to perform hypothesis driven analysis of in-situ debris flow measurements
• You will perform field work to install and operate the systems, as well as to understand sediment transfer at the five study sites
• You will combine all this knowledge to develop new ways to understand and manage debris flows

jobs.description:
Doctoral Positions in Robot Learning and Soft, Musculoskeletal, and Biohybrid Robotics

100%, Zurich, fixed-term

The Soft Robotics Lab within the Institute of Robotics and Intelligent Systems at ETH Zurich is inviting applications for several doctoral positions. Our lab's goal is to build, model, and control robots in a fundamentally different way, so that they become more flexible, dexterous, capable, and adapt better to their environment. We work along four directions: soft and musculoskeletal robotics, biohybrid living systems, dexterous manipulation and robot learning, and simulation for embodied AI. We are looking for exceptional candidates in any of them. This round we especially want two profiles: people who design and build the robots, and people who make policies run on them.

We do not hire against a narrow project description. Your thesis topic is something we shape together in your first months. Tell us which of our directions pulls at you, and what you would want to build.

Project background

Today's robots are mostly rigid, fragile, and a world apart from the agility and resilience of biological bodies. Our bet is that the next generation of robots will be soft, musculoskeletal, and in part alive. They will be built to make contact with the real world rather than to avoid it. We pursue this across four directions, and a strong candidate will find a home in one of them and borrow from the others.

Soft and musculoskeletal robotics. We build bodies from compliant structures, bones, joints, and tendon-like actuation. Our electrohydraulic musculoskeletal leg jumps, moves fast, and adapts to terrain at roughly 1.2% of the energy a motor-driven leg needs ( Nature Communications, 2024 ). Our low-voltage HASEL actuators run near 1100 V, are safe to touch, and work untethered and underwater ( Science Advances, 2024 ). We recently extended these muscles to full antagonistic motion ranges ( ICRA 2025 ) and to a sensorless, inherently compliant anthropomorphic hand driven entirely by electrohydraulic actuation ( IROS 2026 ).

Biohybrid living systems. We grow engineered muscle and use it to actuate machines. We bioprinted multicellular muscle-tendon units that transmit force along a real musculoskeletal path ( Science Advances, 2025 ), embedded sensors directly into muscle for closed-loop control of proprioceptive biohybrid robots ( Advanced Intelligent Systems, 2025 ), and established functional volumetric bioprinting with xolography ( Advanced Materials, 2026 ). Co-optimized volumetric muscle designs for large dynamic deformations are in press at Nature Communications (Balciunaite et al., 2026). The same fabrication line reaches clinical work: with University Hospital Zurich we printed implantable reinforced cardiac tissue patches ( Advanced Materials, 2025 ).

Dexterous manipulation and robot learning. We build hands and the policies that run them. One of our initial hand designs is now commercialized through our spin-off Mimic Robotics . ORCA is our open-source, reliable, and cost-effective anthropomorphic hand for uninterrupted dexterous task learning ( IROS 2025 ). On that hardware we work on imitation learning and diffusion policies, cross-embodiment skill transfer through latent action diffusion (ICRA 2026), sample-efficient reinforcement learning and policy fine-tuning directly on the real robot , vision-language-action models for contact-rich tasks, and tactile representation learning on our high-resolution sensorized skin (ICRA 2024). We also build controllable dexterous world models for training and evaluation, and a benchmark of dexterity for anthropomorphic hands . Whichever side you come from, the offer is the same: the hand, the skin, the simulator, and the people who designed all three sit in one room. Build a mechanism here and someone will have a policy running on it within weeks. Build a policy here and you can change the mechanism when the mechanism is what is wrong.

Simulation, fabrication, and embodied AI. Building these robots requires tools that did not exist. Vision-Controlled Jetting prints rigid skeletons, soft tissue, tendons, and sensors in one pass, including a full musculoskeletal hand and forearm ( Nature, 2023 ). We close the sim-to-real gap with learned residual physics ( RA-L, 2024, Best Paper Award ), and we released SORS , a modular high-fidelity soft-robot simulator, at RoboSoft 2026.

Underwater and aerial systems run through all of this, from SoFi and tendon-driven swimmer digital twins to our open-source soft aerial manipulation platform ( CoRL 2024 ).

Job description

Depending on your direction, your work will emphasize different parts of the following. All of it happens in a lab where hardware, biology, and learning sit in the same room.
• You will take a research idea from concept to a working system: designing the architecture, building it, integrating sensing and control, and validating it through systematic real-world experiments
• If your focus is systems design, you will design and build the robots themselves: mechanisms and compliant structures, actuators and tendon routing, embedded electronics and motor control, and the sensor integration that makes a machine measurable. You will own a system from CAD through fabrication to hardware that still runs six months later
• If your focus is learning, you will develop policies and perception that run on real, compliant, contact-rich hardware: imitation learning, real-world reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, sim-to-real transfer, and multimodal representations that use touch as well as vision. You will help define the benchmarks that make such claims measurable
• Each design cycle feeds the next, so rapid prototyping, measurement, and iteration sit at the heart of every project
• Drawing inspiration from biological musculoskeletal systems, you will engineer how bones, joints, tendons, and muscles can be recreated with compliant materials, artificial actuators, or living tissue, and how their interplay produces strength, dexterity, and robustness
• You will build robots that derive much of their capability from their embodiment, achieving rich, adaptive behavior with less reliance on complex centralized control
• If your focus is biohybrid systems, you will work in our biological laboratories at ETH, culturing and bioprinting tissue and turning it into a controllable actuator
• You will publish at the top venues in the field, release open-source hardware and code where it helps the community, and present your work internationally
• You will supervise semester and Master's projects, which is how most of our doctoral students learn to lead work, and you will collaborate day to day across our hardware, muscles, and machine learning teams
• You will complete a doctorate at ETH Zurich alongside the research, including the coursework of the D-MAVT doctoral programme and a share of teaching in one of our courses

Profile
• You are curious, highly motivated, and independent, and you want to make a real difference with your research
• You work best in a team. You are respectful, and you thrive when you can collaborate with others and support them

Through your prior experience, you have ideally already demonstrated:
• A completed or nearly completed Master's degree in mechanical engineering, robotics, mechatronics, electrical engineering, computer science, materials science, bioengineering, or a closely related field
• Depth in at least one of: hands-on system building and mechatronics (CAD, FEA, 3D printing, machining, molding, electronics, motor control, robot integration), machine learning and control for real robots, soft or bio-inspired materials and actuators, tissue engineering and biofabrication, or physics-based simulation
• Evidence that you carry work through to reality. In a thesis, a semester project, a competition team, or an internship, you have taken something from first idea to a result that worked on real hardware, not only to a simulation benchmark
• Substantial project or thesis work we can read, and ideally a publication or preprint, though we do not expect one at this stage
• Strong written and spoken English, and comfort explaining your work clearly
• Strong motivation for interdisciplinary, experimental research and the curiosity to develop new skills throughout the doctorate
• A collaborative, supportive mindset and the drive to make a real difference with your research
• A clear idea of what you would want to work on with us, and why it matters

Nobody arrives with all of this. Show us the few things you are already good at and the appetite to learn the rest.

We offer
• Supervision that is actually available: weekly one-on-one meetings, a lab that sits in one space, and co-supervision from senior doctoral students and postdocs in your direction
• A conference travel budget, so you present your own work at ICRA, IROS, CoRL, RSS, RoboSoft, or the venue that fits your topic, and you go more than once
• A world-class lab with state-of-the-art fabrication and test facilities: in-house multi-material 3D printing, a machine shop, an electronics lab, our own biological laboratories, over 20 dexterous robotic hands and 12 robot arms for real-world data collection and teleoperation, high-resolution tactile skins, and a dedicated GPU cluster with eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs alongside access to ETH's central compute and the Alps supercomputer at CSCS
• A multidisciplinary team of mechanical engineers, materials scientists, biologists, and machine learning researchers, embedded in the broader robotics ecosystem at ETH Zurich
• Strong ties to industry and to our spin-offs, and support for turning your research into something that leaves the lab. Our doctoral graduates have gone to faculty positions, to top industry labs, and into founding companies
• Your job with impact: become part of ETH Zurich, which not only supports your professional development, but also actively contributes to positive change in society
• You can expect numerous benefits , such as public transport season tickets and car sharing, a wide range of sports offered by the ASVZ , childcare and attractive pension benefits
• A fully funded doctoral position paid at ETH Zurich highly competitive doctoral salary rate . This is a salaried employment contract with full social benefits, not a stipend
• An initial contract of 18 months, extended annually after that

We value diversity and sustainability

In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. We promote equality of opportunity, value diversity and nurture a working and learning environment in which the rights and dignity of all our staff and students are respected. Visit our Equal Opportunities and Diversity website to find out how we ensure a fair and open environment that allows everyone to grow and flourish. Sustainability is a core value for us – we are consistently working towards a climate-neutral future .

Curious? So are we.

We look forward to receiving your online application with the following documents as a single merged PDF document, ideally under 10 MB and no larger than 40 MB, titled with your last name and initials as well as the application date (for example, 20260901_DoeJane_application) in the following order:
• Cover letter addressed to Prof. Robert Katzschmann, describing what you have built, which of our directions you want to work in, and why. One to two pages
• Detailed CV, including a list of any publications or preprints
• Transcripts of all degrees in English, with the local grading scale, which ETH requires for doctoral admission
• Your Master's thesis or a representative project report, in English. A draft or an in-progress version is fine if you have not finished yet
• Up to two of your publications or preprints, if you have them. We do not expect publications at this stage, but if you have written something we would like to read it
• Names and contact information of at least two references, usually your thesis supervisor. Reference letters are optional

Please upload one PDF only, not several separate files.

Further information about our group can be found on our website . Questions regarding the position should be directed to Federica Poltronieri, federica.poltronieri@srl.ethz.ch (no applications).

Please note that we exclusively accept applications submitted through our online application portal. Applications via email or postal services will not be considered.

Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis until November 30, 2026. We have several doctoral positions to fill in the coming months. Start date by agreement.

We aim to respond within three weeks. The process has three steps: a first interview and a technical deep dive, both online, and finally a lab visit in Zurich.

We are also hiring postdoctoral researchers .
